requirements.requirement: Join node2's and node3's segments into a single L2 domain via a bridge/forwarding device on node1
requirements.summary: node1's eth1 (toward node2) and eth2 (toward node3) were enslaved into a new Linux bridge br0 with STP disabled, replacing the prior separate-segment routed setup. Confirmed by bridge link show output showing both interfaces in 'forwarding' state under br0.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 share one subnet
requirements.summary: node2's ens7 assigned 192.168.50.11/24 and node3's ens7 assigned 192.168.50.12/24, both in the same /24 subnet, persisted in /etc/network/interfaces.d/60-ens7.cfg on each host.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 reach each other directly at layer 2 (node1 forwards frames, does not appear as an L3 hop)
requirements.summary: node2's ARP table for ens7 shows node3's real interface MAC (02:c0:b2:8a:e0:f1) directly, and vice versa on node3 (02:d9:fa:7a:c6:ef) — matching each host's own ens7 hardware address rather than any node1 MAC, which is the signature of transparent bridging rather than routing. ICMP TTL remained 64 (unchanged) in ping tests, consistent with a non-routed L2 hop.

requirements.requirement: node1 performs pure frame forwarding, not routing (no IP on the joining interface/bridge)
requirements.summary: br0 was confirmed to carry no IPv4 address ('br0 should have no IP - node1 not a routed hop' check returned nothing), and eth1/eth2 addresses were flushed before bridging, consistent with pure L2 forwarding.

requirements.requirement: Bridge/IP configuration and connectivity survive node restarts (persistence across reboot)
requirements.summary: Healthy baseline was captured pre-restart (boot_ids, bridge forwarding state, working pings) for all three nodes. Each node was rebooted individually; boot_id changed on each (node1: 6cef3db6→2dc313d8, node2: 35c87ec9→75267425, node3: a9593011→92c2d8c9), confirming a real restart occurred. After node1's reboot, the l2-bridge.service unit ran and recreated br0 with eth1/eth2 forwarding and no IP, and after all three nodes were back up, node2↔node3 ping succeeded and ARP again showed direct peer MACs, demonstrating full end-to-end recovery of the L2 domain.

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes — merging node2's and node3's separate segments into one L2 domain via a node1 bridge, giving node2/node3 a shared subnet, and demonstrating transparent frame forwarding (not routing) by node1 — are all directly supported by evidence: bridge creation, matching subnet assignment, ARP tables showing each host's real peer MAC address, unchanged ICMP TTL, and an addressless br0. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also satisfied for all three nodes, with pre-restart healthy baselines, changed boot IDs after each reboot, and full post-restart recovery of the bridge and end-to-end connectivity, directly observed rather than only inferred from configuration. Hygiene is good overall; a couple of unrequested, low-risk, non-destructive mutations (docker0 cleanup baked into the persistent boot script, and a defensive but ultimately unneeded service stop) are noted but did not harm functionality or leave failed/insecure state.
limitations: The exact eth1↔node2 / eth2↔node3 physical mapping was inferred partly by elimination (traffic seen only on eth1, absence on eth2) rather than a direct capture of node3's traffic on eth2, though the final bidirectional ping and ARP checks after full bridging independently confirm the joined domain functions correctly regardless of the initial mapping guess.

The l2-bridge.service state immediately after node1's reboot briefly showed 'inactive' and br0 'does not exist' (cmd-cc1be06b439c4d7d) before the follow-up check ~3s later showed it active and successful (cmd-275d6b79b0484e56); this is most plausibly a timing/race artifact of polling immediately after SSH access returned, but the trace does not include a poll loop with timestamps proving the transition was a benign boot-order effect rather than a onetime failure that self-corrected.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands trace cleanly to task prerequisites, evidence collection, or restoration. Diagnostic tcpdump captures used to empirically map eth1/eth2 to node2/node3 (cmd-d0d8120a249747e7, cmd-540b6faa3ca648c9) left temp files that were subsequently cleaned up (cmd-d34d3c517eb94c8d), a fully reverted, bounded, low-risk action. One unrequested but low-risk mutation: while setting up the bridge, the executor also removed docker0's stray class-E IP and set it down (part of cmd-92f1d627c2814541, and baked permanently into the persisted l2-bridge-setup.sh script run at every boot). This was not required by the task; docker0 was already carrier-down and unused by the running SONiC containers, so the mutation is low-risk and did not damage functionality, but it is scope beyond the stated requirement and now runs on every future boot via the systemd unit. Stopping interfaces-config.service/networking.service before building the bridge (also in cmd-92f1d627c2814541) was a defensive precaution the executor's own investigation later showed was unnecessary (those services only manage eth0), though it was not re-disabled or left in a broken state. No destructive, unbounded, or security-weakening actions were observed; package state and other services were left healthy per the after_executor snapshot.
